readerTitle: The $1 million offer that might be the wrong size
caseNote: 가상 사례 (독립 철물점용 재고 앱 스타트업, 엔지니어링 번역 에이전시) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 투자를 받을지 말지는 지분을 얼마나 내주느냐보다, 그 돈이 요구하는 성장을 내 시장과 계획이 감당할 수 있느냐로 판단한다.
misconception: 좋은 조건의 투자 제안이 오면 받는 게 이득이다. 지분 20%를 팔면 창업자는 계속 80%를 가진다.

sources.text: 벤처 투자와 지분 희석의 표준 개념 (프리머니·포스트머니 가치, 라운드별 희석)

factChecks.note: "벤처 펀드는 소수의 큰 성공이 다수의 실패를 메운다"는 일반적 설명으로만 썼습니다. 구체적 비율이나 통계는 넣지 않았습니다.
다음 레슨 예고(Mailchimp, 외부 투자 없이 성장, 약 $12B 매각)는 FIN-07-09 내용과 맞는지 게시 전 확인하세요.

cards.title: The $1 million offer that might be the wrong size
body: Priya built an app that tells independent hardware stores what to reorder and when. Forty stores pay her $150 a month. It's growing, slowly.
Then an investor offers **$1 million for 20%** of the company. Her co-founder says take it tonight. Priya isn't sure what she'd be agreeing to.

image.label: Founder at a kitchen table with a term sheet and a laptop
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 밤의 부엌 식탁, 노트북 화면에 재고 그래프, 옆에 "$1,000,000 for 20%"라고 적힌 서류 한 장. 창밖에 작은 철물점 간판(실제 상호·로고 없음).

options.text: Sign. $1 million for 20% is a strong price for a company this small
options.feedback: The price may be fine, but she'd be accepting growth targets she hasn't asked about. That's **what investors expect**, and it matters more than the headline number.

options.text: Ask what the investor needs the company to become, then check it against her market
options.feedback: This tests whether her business can deliver the outcome the money is built for. It costs a few days, not the deal.

options.text: Decline. Outside money means losing control
options.feedback: She keeps full ownership, but she might also miss the cash to grow before a rival does. Saying no without the math is as blind as saying yes.

cards.title: 20% is rarely the last 20%.
body: Most venture-backed companies raise again. Say Priya sells 20% in each of three rounds. Each round takes a fifth of what she has *left*, not of what she started with. That's **dilution**: her share shrinks every time new shares go to new investors.

cards.title: A smaller slice only wins if the pie grows.
body: Today the company might be worth $3 million. All of it is hers: $3 million on paper.
If the money helps it reach $30 million, her 51% is worth about $15 million. Dilution paid off.

If growth stalls and the company is worth $4 million, her 51% is worth about $2 million. She'd own half of something barely bigger than before. **Dilution is a bet that each round grows the company faster than her share shrinks.**

image.label: Three pies: small whole pie, big pie with half slice, small pie with half slice
image.brief: 파이 그림 3개 나란히. 왼쪽 작은 파이 전체 "100% of $3M", 가운데 큰 파이의 절반 "51% of $30M", 오른쪽 작은 파이의 절반 "51% of $4M". 가운데만 밝은 색으로 강조.

cards.title: Check the money's math, not just yours.
body: $1 million for 20% values the company at $5 million after the money arrives. A venture fund backs many companies, knowing most will fail. The few big winners must pay for the rest. So each company needs a path to being worth many times the entry price.

Now Priya's side. Say 3,000 stores could ever use her app. At $150 a month, that's **$5.4 million a year**, even if she won every single one. A good business, but likely too small for this kind of money unless she expands to new markets.

cards.title: Percentages hide the terms.
body: Two offers with the same valuation can be very different deals. One may add a board seat, veto rights or a rule that investors get their money back first if the company sells.
And growth expectations don't fade after signing. Money raised for fast growth usually has to be spent on fast growth. Read the terms before comparing the numbers.

cards.title: Now it's a translation agency.
body: Lena runs a profitable agency that translates manuals for engineering firms: $1.2 million a year in sales, growing steadily. She's building software so her translators work faster. Maybe she'll license it to a few agencies later.
Offer 1: a venture fund, $2 million for 25%, expecting revenue to triple in two years. Offer 2: an angel, $400,000 for 8%, happy with steady growth.

options.text: Take the $2 million. More money means more options
options.feedback: She gets a bigger cushion but signs up for tripling sales, which her plan doesn't aim for. That gap between plan and **investor expectations** is where the trouble starts.

options.text: Take the $400,000, which fits the plan she actually has
options.feedback: She gives up 8% instead of 25%, so **dilution** stays small, and her backer expects what she plans to deliver. The cost: a slower build if the software takes off.

options.text: Take the $2 million and decide about growth later
options.feedback: The terms decide that for her. She'd hand over a quarter of a profitable firm for a growth promise she hasn't chosen.

cards.title: Raise the money your business can actually grow into.
body: Two ideas did the work today. **Dilution:** each round shrinks your share, so it only pays if the company grows faster. **What investors expect:** every check comes with an outcome it needs, and your market has to be big enough to deliver it.
**Try it today:** estimate the most your business could earn if it won every possible customer. Compare that with what a big funding round would need it to become.
